_README: AUTHORED EXPLANATIONS. Hand-written, applied by apply-migration.mjs step 8.
`why` is what a reader sees after getting a drill card wrong. The engine already
synthesises a floor line from the card itself (the correct option, the pairs or
blanks missed) and links through to the Brief, so these do NOT restate the answer.
They give the reasoning, name the trap, or separate the two things being confused.
`model` is the 💡 line under a written answer's marking points — what else earns
credit, or how to structure the answer. Never a replacement for `points`.
k : the card key — hash(type | question | content signature), the same ckey
apply-migration.mjs uses to dedupe. Edit a question and its key changes, so
a stale entry cannot silently attach itself to the wrong card: the gate in
apply-migration.mjs fails the build on any key that resolves to no card.
q : a verbatim fragment of anything the card puts on screen — its question, its
passage, an option, a pair prompt — checked as a substring. A human anchor,
and a second guard against a hash collision. It has to reach past the
question because three `match` cards share the question "Match each statement
to the correct term from Hannetjie's wordlist" and only their pairs differ.
t : the text. HTML is allowed; <b> marks the discriminator.
A FEW ENTRIES FLAG A CONTRADICTION IN THE COURSE MATERIAL rather than teaching
around it. Verbatim cards reproduce the lecturer's own key and are never edited —
so where that key and the standard rule disagree, the explanation says so and
teaches the rule. The three substantive ones are tabled in ../README.md; a fourth
is a naming slip (an option list treating the bundle of His and the
atrioventricular bundle as two separate steps).
No third-person pronouns for the lecturer: apply-migration.mjs re-scans `why` and
`model` and fails the build on one.

why.q: Match each substance to what the cardiovascular system does
why.t: The theme is transport. Every one of these is the same system moving something from where it is made or absorbed to where it is used or excreted — note that urea travels liver to kidney, not the other way.

why.q: A measure which shows how easy or hard it is for air/blood to flow
why.t: These five words are the vocabulary the whole blood-flow section is built on. Resistance is how hard flow is, constriction is the smooth-muscle narrowing that raises it, and perfusion is the result — blood actually reaching the tissue.

why.q: This is where the RAAS system is activated
why.t: Follow the chain in order and every blank sits somewhere on it: renin from the kidney acts on angiotensinogen from the liver, ACE in the lung makes angiotensin II, and angiotensin II then triggers aldosterone (sodium reabsorbed, water follows) and ADH (water reabsorbed directly).

why.q: How is the structure of the artery different to that of the vein
why.t: One rule generates the whole table. The artery must withstand pressure, so its media and elastic laminae are thick and prominent around a small round lumen; the vein only carries volume back, so it is floppy with a large lumen and a thick outer coat.

why.q: The nurse explains to him that these measurements show that he has
why.t: Two ideas cover almost all of it: BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance, and pressure is sensed by baroreceptors (aortic arch and carotid sinus) while blood chemistry is sensed by chemoreceptors (aortic and carotid bodies). Confusing those two receptor sets is the trap, and it is set here twice.

why.q: Match each vessel feature to the vessel it belongs to
why.t: Read the wall and the vessel names itself: elastic media means pressure (artery), valves mean flow against gravity (vein), one cell thick means exchange (capillary).

why.q: forming a tight barrier between the blood and the nervous tissue
why.t: Capillary type follows the job of the organ: continuous where nothing may leak (brain), fenestrated where small molecules must filter out (kidney), sinusoidal where whole cells must cross (bone marrow). The rest is just right ventricle to lungs, left ventricle to body.

why.q: Blood is pumped to the lungs and body tissues through
why.t: The layer names are built from their position — endocardium lines the inside, so it is what the valves are made of; myocardium is the muscle. Same logic names the septa for the chambers they sit between.

why.q: One of the underlined terms is incorrect
why.t: Blood pressure is defined and measured in the arteries — that is the only planted error. The rest of that answer is the standard definition, including pulse pressure as the gap between the two readings.

why.q: The answer below contains two errors in the underlined parts
why.t: Neither error is in the physiology, and both matter anyway: cardiac output is per minute, and stroke volume is quoted for the left ventricle. Get the first wrong and every calculation built on CO = HR × SV comes out wrong with it.

why.q: Correctly identify the structures in the image below by matching the letters
why.t: Work outwards from the lumen — intima, media, externa — then use shape to tell the vessels apart: thick-walled and round is the artery, floppy with a valve is the vein, a single-layer tube is the capillary.

why.q: which conduct blood toward the heart, regardless of oxygen content
why.t: The definition is about direction, not oxygen. Veins run towards the heart even when the blood in them is oxygenated, which is exactly what the pulmonary veins do.

why.q: which are responsible for the exchange of gases and nutrients
why.t: Exchange needs a wall one cell thick and slow flow. Only the capillary has both — everything else is plumbing.

why.q: which is the most critical in regulating systemic blood pressure
why.t: The smooth muscle in the media is what changes a vessel's diameter, and diameter is what sets peripheral resistance — the other half of BP = CO × PR.

why.q: actively causes vasoconstriction and vasodilation
why.t: Same point again: only the media has smooth muscle. The endothelium can signal a vessel to relax (nitric oxide), but it cannot contract.

why.q: Why can’t you feel a pulse in a vein
why.t: A pulse is the pressure wave from ventricular ejection, and the capillary bed damps it out before the blood reaches any vein. Thin walls are a consequence of low pressure, not the reason the pulse is missing.

why.q: The effects of venous return, plasma electrolytes, stress, and exercise
why.t: Everything here routes through CO = SV × HR and then BP = CO × PR. Calcium raises contractility, potassium slows the heart, and the trained heart pumps slower but more forcefully — the same output in fewer beats.

why.q: Her nervous system helps to lower blood pressure back to normal
why.t: The reflex always runs receptor → centre → nerve → effector → result: baroreceptors fire, the cardio-inhibitory centre is stimulated, the vagus releases acetylcholine at the SA node, rate falls, pressure falls. The vasomotor centre does the other half by relaxing vessel smooth muscle.

why.q: Mesenteric adenitis is usually a mild condition
why.t: Two facts unlock most of the blanks: MALT is lymphoid tissue sitting in mucosal membranes, so organs like the spleen and thymus are not MALT; and the lymphatic system's main job is fluid balance — immunity is what it does with that fluid on the way past. One warning about the key on the cell-function blank. The abundant cell in lymph is the lymphocyte, and that part is right — but this paper then marks its function as "primary mediators of the rapid innate host defense", which is the description of a neutrophil. Lymphocytes are the adaptive arm: B cells make antibody, T cells kill infected cells and direct the response. Answer the key to score the mark here, and hold on to the real division — innate and fast is the neutrophil, specific and remembered is the lymphocyte.

why.q: Describe the forces acting across a blood capillary
why.t: The whole card is one tug-of-war: hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out at the arteriolar end, and oncotic pressure pulls it back at the venular end because the plasma proteins stayed behind. The fluid leaves into the interstitium, the space between the cells.

why.q: What will happen to fluid movement in the following conditions
why.t: Albumin is what creates the oncotic pull, so losing it makes that pull weaker, not stronger — less fluid is drawn back in and oedema follows. That is the planted error, and it is the mechanism behind the swollen abdomen of severe malnutrition.

why.q: Describe the direct renal control of BP
why.t: Trace it as a volume story: low BP means less blood reaching the kidney, so less filtrate and less urine, so volume is kept, so venous return and stroke volume rise and push pressure back up. Both planted errors run that chain backwards.

why.q: Answer the question to ensure that the conditions and their descriptions match
why.t: The word-parts do most of the work: -oedema is fluid, -itis is inflammation, -adenopathy is any node disease, -oma is a tumour. Only elephantiasis (a parasitic worm) and buboes have to be learned as plain facts.

why.q: The primary mechanism driving filtration in capillary beds
why.t: Filtration is driven by the pressure inside the capillary — the heart's push, still present at the arteriolar end. Osmotic and oncotic pressure work the other way, pulling fluid back in.

why.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the lymphatic system
why.t: The three real ones are fluid balance, absorbing fat from the gut, and immunity. Blood sugar is endocrine — pancreas and liver — and has nothing to do with lymph.

why.q: higher osmolality than the fluid within a red blood cell
why.t: Only water moves here. When the solute concentration differs across a membrane, water crosses towards the more concentrated side until they match — no carrier, no energy, so it is osmosis rather than any form of diffusion or transport.

why.q: The effect of general factors on blood pressure
why.t: Sort every chemical by which half of BP = CO × PR it touches: ANP and nitric oxide drop volume or dilate vessels, adrenaline and ADH raise rate or hold water back. And peripheral resistance itself depends on vessel length and diameter, not on the heart at all.

why.q: Match each change to its effect on blood pressure
why.t: Everything routes through BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance: vessel diameter and blood viscosity move the resistance term, blood volume moves the cardiac output term.

why.q: Describe the body’s neural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure
why.t: Baroreceptors sense stretch, which means pressure; chemoreceptors sense chemistry. Their addresses differ too — baroreceptors in the aortic arch and the carotid sinus, chemoreceptors in the aortic and carotid bodies. Both planted errors are that same swap.

why.q: Predict the change in peripheral resistance as blood vessel diameter
why.t: Resistance falls very steeply as a vessel widens — a small change in diameter does far more to flow than any change in vessel length or blood viscosity. That is why the arterioles, not the arteries, are the resistance vessels.

why.q: Write a formula showing the relationship between BP, CO & SVR
why.t: Pressure is what you get when flow meets resistance, so the two multiply. Rearranged the other way, CO = BP ÷ SVR — worth being able to do in either direction.

why.q: changes to the heart you can detect by examining an ECG
why.t: An ECG records electrical activity only. Rate, rhythm and injury patterns are electrical; pressure, resistance and the volume actually pumped are mechanical, and no trace can show them.

why.q: The homeostatic mechanisms involved in the control of heart rate
why.t: Two spines hold this up. Anatomy: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres. Control: sympathetic nerves and noradrenaline speed the SA node up, the vagus and acetylcholine slow it down. The cycle-length blank is arithmetic — sixty seconds divided by the rate.

why.q: Lagi has an ECG to check his heart function
why.t: The order follows the anatomy, and the step people drop is the one in the middle: the atrial myocardium spreads the impulse cell to cell through intercalated discs before the AV node holds it up.

why.q: concerned about the anchorage of his atrioventricular valves
why.t: The papillary muscles anchor the chordae tendineae, and they tighten just before the ventricle contracts — so the valve cusps cannot blow back into the atrium under pressure.

why.q: The sounds of his heart shows a murmur between the lub and dub
why.t: Heart sounds are valves closing, not muscle contracting. A murmur between lub and dub is therefore blood crossing a valve that should be shut — in mitral regurgitation, back into the left atrium while the ventricle contracts.

why.q: the blood vessel labelled X is the
why.t: Follow the drainage upstream: the jugular vein drains the head and empties into the subclavian, and the two together become the brachiocephalic vein before the superior vena cava.

why.q: Match each heart structure to its description
why.t: The prefixes place them: endo- inside, myo- muscle, peri- around. Chordae tendineae and the septa are named for what they hold and what they separate.

why.q: Using the superior view of the valves
why.t: Name each valve by what is downstream of it — the pulmonary valve guards the pulmonary trunk, the aortic valve the aorta. The two AV valves are told apart by side: tricuspid right, mitral left.

why.q: Match the different parts of an ECG wave
why.t: Depolarisation comes before repolarisation, and atria before ventricles: P, then QRS, then T. Atrial repolarisation does happen — it is just buried inside the QRS, which is why there is no wave for it.

why.q: Match the progress of the electrical impulse through the heart
why.t: The flat parts matter as much as the spikes. The PR segment is the AV node delay that lets the atria finish filling the ventricles, and the ST segment is the ventricles fully depolarised and contracting — which is why it shifts in a STEMI.

why.q: Match the names with the numbers on the diagram
why.t: Work through the flow rather than memorising numbers: right atrium, tricuspid, right ventricle, pulmonary valve on one side; left ventricle, aortic valve, aortic arch on the other.

why.q: The pumping chambers of the heart are the
why.t: Systole is contraction, diastole is the filling pause — the two halves of every cardiac cycle. Stroke volume is simply what one systole manages to eject.

why.q: The larger partition between the two sides of the heart
why.t: Two cusps means bicuspid, which is the mitral valve. And the coronary arteries feed the myocardium — which is why blocking one kills muscle rather than lining.

why.q: Label the five components of the conduction system
why.t: It is the same chain top to bottom every time — SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres — so the labels run in that order down the diagram.

why.q: Explain what the following waves of the ECG represent
why.t: Every wave on an ECG is a voltage change, not a contraction, and a chamber must depolarise before it can contract. That one word is the planted error.

why.q: Explain the meanings of cardiac reserve and ejection fraction
why.t: Cardiac reserve is about output — how much more the heart can pump than it does at rest — and ejection fraction is quoted for the left ventricle, because that is the side whose failure gets measured clinically.

why.q: understanding of the terms chronotropic and inotropic
why.t: Chrono means time, so rate; ino means force. Sympathetic stimulation and noradrenaline raise both, by driving more calcium into the myocardial cells; acetylcholine from the vagus lowers rate.

why.q: These kinds of shock are directly linked to the heart
why.t: Group shock by what has failed: pump (cardiogenic), volume (hypovolaemic), vessel tone (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), or a physical block to filling or ejection — tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive clot — which is obstructive.

why.q: The homeostatic mechanisms that are involved in stroke volume
why.t: Everything else on the list either fills the ventricle more (venous return, blood volume) or makes it squeeze harder (adrenaline, sympathetic drive, calcium). Raised potassium does the opposite — it depresses the myocardium and slows conduction.

why.q: Which kind of blood vessels have valves to prevent backflow
why.t: Valves are needed wherever pressure is too low to keep blood moving one way on its own. That is the veins, especially in the limbs, where the skeletal muscle pump does the pushing.

why.q: The trabeculae carneae muscles in the ventricles
why.t: Trabeculae carneae are the muscular ridges lining the ventricles. Do not confuse them with the chordae tendineae, the thread-like cords that hold the valve cusps down.

why.q: Exercise ...
why.t: The skeletal muscle pump and deeper breathing push more blood back to the heart; a fuller ventricle stretches further and contracts harder. That is Starling's law, and it is why a trained heart can pump more per beat.

why.q: the flow of blood in the INCORRECT sequence
why.t: Check any sequence against the single loop: body → vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → mitral → left ventricle → aorta. The odd one out puts a chamber or a valve out of that order.

why.q: The mitral valve has two large cusps
why.t: Bicuspid is the other name for it — two cusps on the left, three on the right. The names are simply a count.

why.q: The openings to the coronary arteries open when the aortic valve closes
why.t: The heart feeds itself in diastole. While the aortic valve is open its cusps sit over the coronary openings; only when it shuts does blood recoil back and enter them — which is why a very fast heart rate starves the myocardium.

why.q: The LAD artery is also known as the widow maker
why.t: The left anterior descending supplies most of the left ventricle and the septum, so occluding it takes out the muscle the body cannot manage without.

why.q: An opening between the atria in the heart that closes to become
why.t: Every fetal shunt bypasses something not yet working: the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus bypass the lungs, the ductus venosus bypasses the liver. Each leaves a ligament or a dimple behind after birth.

why.q: prevent back-flow of blood when the ventricles contract
why.t: The two sets of valves always work in opposition. When the ventricles contract the AV valves shut — that is the first heart sound — and the semilunar valves open.

why.q: Which layer of the heart use the most energy
why.t: It is the only layer that does mechanical work, contracting every second of a lifetime. That is also why it gets its own arterial supply rather than living off the blood inside the chambers.

why.q: The following statement about the heart is true
why.t: The three wrong options are all near-misses worth learning: the septum is muscle, the fossa ovalis sits in the inter-atrial septum, and the tricuspid is an AV valve, not a semilunar one.

why.q: electrical conduction system is true
why.t: The route never varies, always top down: SA node, AV node, then the bundle and its branches, then the Purkinje fibres. An option that starts at the AV node is describing an escape rhythm, not the normal path. (Note the option lists the bundle of His and the atrioventricular bundle as separate steps — they are two names for the same structure.)

why.q: automaticity
why.t: This is why a transplanted heart still beats. The SA node leads simply because it depolarises fastest; nerves and hormones only speed that up or slow it down.

why.q: refracticity
why.t: The long refractory period is protective: cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised the way skeletal muscle can, so the ventricle is forced to relax and refill between beats.

why.q: During depolarisation sodium ions move into the myocardial cells
why.t: Depolarisation is sodium rushing in, cancelling the negative charge inside the cell. The waves on the trace then just report where in the heart that is happening.

why.q: if the force of contraction (myocardial contractility)
why.t: Adrenaline drives more calcium into the myocardial cell, the fibres shorten further within the same beat, and more of what is in the ventricle gets ejected — a bigger stroke volume from the same filling.

why.q: What is the potential space between the two lungs called
why.t: The mediastinum is the space between the lungs that holds the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus. Pleura and pericardium are membranes, not spaces.

why.q: The membrane that forms the shiny layer on the lung surface
why.t: Visceral means on the organ — the same word is used of the pericardium and the peritoneum. Parietal is always the layer lining the wall.

why.q: The double membrane that surrounds the lung
why.t: Same rule, in order: the membrane as a whole is the pleura, the layer stuck to the lung is visceral, and the layer lining the thoracic wall is parietal. The film of fluid between them is what stops the lung pulling away.

why.q: Hyperbaric chambers are clinical applications of which gas law
why.t: The chamber itself works by compressing gas — pressure up, volume down — which is Boyle. Henry's law is what then explains the extra oxygen dissolving into the blood, so read carefully which half of the process a question is asking about.

why.q: Blood from inside this structure will next flow into what other structure
why.t: If the next stop is a ventricle, what you are looking at must be an atrium — on both sides blood runs atrium → ventricle → artery, never backwards.

why.q: A trauma patient is progressing rapidly into circulatory shock
why.t: Two clues drive it. A bruised abdomen with no visible bleeding points to concealed haemorrhage, and neck pain in a trauma patient raises a cervical cord injury, which removes sympathetic tone and lets the vessels dilate. Afebrile rules out sepsis, and no drug was given.

why.q: Cardiogenic shock can be caused by
why.t: Cardiogenic means the pump itself cannot deliver — the coronary clot starves the muscle, the pericardial fluid stops the ventricle filling. Be aware that another past question in this pack files pericardial fluid under obstructive shock; both labels are used in the course material, so read the stem before choosing.

why.q: Match the names with the numbers on the diagram
why.t: Use position rather than the numbers: the two venae cavae enter the right atrium from above and below, the pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle, and the pulmonary veins come back into the left atrium.

why.q: Anatomical Structures of the Heart Identify the structures
why.t: The branches off the arch run right to left: brachiocephalic first, then left common carotid, then left subclavian. The brachiocephalic is the only one that divides again, which is what makes it recognisable.

why.q: What is a coronary angiogram and what is the purpose
why.t: A coronary angiogram looks at the heart's own arteries; carotid is the neck. The other planted error swaps dissolving a clot with a drug for pulling it out mechanically.

why.q: Blood is returned to the heart via the
why.t: Do not forget the third route: the coronary sinus returns the heart's own venous blood straight into the right atrium, alongside both venae cavae.

why.q: The major vessel delivering deoxygenated blood to the lungs
why.t: It is the one artery carrying deoxygenated blood — vessels are named for the direction they travel, not the blood they hold.

why.q: The pulmonary circulation is a higher pressure circulation
why.t: The pulmonary circuit is short and low pressure, which is why the right ventricle wall is so much thinner. Systemic pressures there would push fluid straight into the alveoli.

why.q: Another name for the left anterior interventricular artery
why.t: They are the two branches of the left coronary artery: the anterior interventricular (the LAD) runs down the front of the septum, the circumflex curves around the left side.

why.q: A blood vessel that allows placental blood to bypass the liver
why.t: Sort the three fetal shunts by what each one skips: ductus venosus the liver, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus the lungs.

why.q: The coronary ostia are found in the
why.t: The coronaries are the first branches off the aorta, just above the aortic valve. The heart supplies itself before anything else gets any blood.

why.q: Name the major blood vessels in the neck
why.t: The question asks for vessels in the neck — the subclavian pair sit under the clavicle, at the shoulder, which is what their name says.

why.q: Match each heart sound to its cause
why.t: Sounds are valves closing: S1 the AV valves at the start of ventricular contraction, S2 the semilunar valves at its end. S3 and S4 are filling sounds — blood rushing in, and the atrium pushing against a stiff ventricle.

why.q: roughly equivalent
why.t: Diffusion depends on the gradient and on solubility. Carbon dioxide is far more soluble in water than oxygen is, so a much smaller pressure gradient still shifts the same amount of gas.

why.q: The poor solubility of oxygen in water
why.t: Only a small fraction of oxygen can dissolve in plasma, nowhere near enough for metabolism, so almost all of it travels bound to haemoglobin. Anaemia limits oxygen delivery for exactly this reason.

why.q: Match each conduction structure to its feature
why.t: Every part of the chain has its own intrinsic rate, and the fastest one sets the pace — normally the SA node. The AV delay is not a flaw: it is what lets the atria empty before the ventricles fire.

why.q: Match each deflection to what it represents
why.t: Read it as depolarise, depolarise, repolarise — atria, then ventricles, then ventricles again — with the P–R interval as the pause at the AV node in between.

why.q: Order the sequence of the flow of electrical impulses
why.t: The same chain every time, and each step earns its place: the AV node delays, the bundle branches carry the signal fast down the septum, and the Purkinje fibres make the ventricles contract from the apex upwards, squeezing blood towards the outflow valves.

why.q: What does an ECG record
why.t: An ECG picks up the whole heart, atria included — the P wave is atrial. Restricting it to ventricular muscle is the planted error.

why.q: Label the ECG recording below
why.t: Read left to right: the small bump is P, then the three parts of the QRS complex (Q down, R up, S down), then the broader T.

why.q: A patient with the following ECG result is going into shock
why.t: An ECG can only show you the pump. If the trace itself explains the shock, the answer is cardiogenic — the other three are diagnosed from the history (an allergen, an infection, an obstruction), not from a rhythm strip.

why.q: often called the pacemaker
why.t: It leads because it depolarises fastest. Every other part of the chain can pace the heart if the SA node fails, just more slowly — which is what an escape rhythm is.

why.q: The short-term homeostatic control of blood pressure
why.t: One reflex, run in both directions. Low BP: sympathetic outflow, faster heart, vasoconstriction, pressure up. High BP: the vagus and acetylcholine slow the heart while the vasomotor centre is inhibited, so vessels dilate. Note the sensors are baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus, not the bodies.

why.q: What is the normal heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output at rest
why.t: The three are tied together by CO = SV × HR — multiply the middle of the first two ranges and the third falls out. Learn the relationship and you can reconstruct any one of them.

why.q: Presence of air in the pleural cavity
why.t: Build them from the parts: dys- difficult, eu- normal, pneumo-thorax air in the chest, cyan- blue. Atelectasis is the odd one out — it names the lung collapsing, whatever caused it.

why.q: Kalama ate a large piece of bread
why.t: The soft back wall of the trachea is the trachealis muscle, and its softness is exactly why a large bolus in the oesophagus behind it can press forward into the airway. The epiglottis is the lid; the ciliated mucous lining is the escalator that stops particles going deeper.

why.q: That allowed air to get into
why.t: Separate the cause from the result: pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, and atelectasis is the lung collapsing because the negative pressure holding it open has been lost.

why.q: lung tissue in a beaker of water
why.t: A lung that has breathed keeps its residual volume — air that cannot be forced out — so it floats. A lung that never inflated has none, and sinks. This is a real forensic test.

why.q: Match each factor to its effect on heart rate
why.t: Everything here is sympathetic drive up or down, with one exception: in endurance training the resting rate falls because a bigger stroke volume delivers the same cardiac output in fewer beats.

why.q: have cartilage in their walls to keep them open
why.t: Cartilage holds the conducting airways open, and it runs out at the bronchioles. That is precisely why bronchioles can constrict in asthma and the trachea cannot.

why.q: The cuboidal epithelium visible in this image
why.t: The epithelium thins as the airway narrows: pseudostratified columnar in the trachea, cuboidal in the bronchiole, simple squamous in the alveolus. Cuboidal cells with no cartilage in the wall is the giveaway.

why.q: This is a section through a trachea
why.t: The trachea does contain hyaline cartilage — but read what the label is actually sitting on. Answering from the organ rather than from the structure the arrow points at is the trap here.

why.q: The pressure exerted by each gas in a mixture is proportional
why.t: Dalton is about a mixture: each gas contributes pressure in proportion to how much of the mixture it makes up. Boyle relates pressure to volume; Henry describes how much gas dissolves in a liquid.

why.q: All of the following statements are true of inspiration except
why.t: Quiet inspiration is active: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the thorax enlarges, and the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric so air moves in. It is quiet expiration that is passive.

why.q: What effect will a decrease in pH have on the respiration rate
why.t: A falling pH means excess hydrogen ions, and blowing off carbon dioxide removes acid. Ventilation rises to correct acidosis — the same reflex behind the deep sighing breaths of diabetic ketoacidosis.

why.q: which factors directly influence a persons lung capacity
why.t: Lung capacity is set by body size and physiology — height, sex and age, plus the reference ranges that are adjusted for ethnic background. The distractors are all social rather than biological.

why.q: if there is increased venous return to the heart
why.t: More filling stretches the ventricle further, and a stretched cardiac fibre contracts more strongly. That is Starling's law, and it is how the heart matches its output to what comes back to it.

why.q: if arterial vessels are constricted
why.t: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle has to beat against. Raise it and less blood leaves per beat — which is why untreated hypertension eventually wears the left ventricle out.

why.q: Match each component of blood pressure regulation
why.t: Two timescales in one list. Baroreceptors and the vasomotor centre act in seconds; renin, aldosterone and ADH work over hours, and they work by changing volume rather than vessel diameter.

why.q: Cold and clammy skin, tachycardia, and rapid breathing
why.t: Cold clammy skin with a racing heart is the classic fight-or-flight picture — vasoconstriction shunting blood to the core. The renin pathway matters in shock too, but it is slower and does not produce these signs.

why.q: Choose the correct cause of each of the following types of shock
why.t: Name the thing that failed: volume (hypovolaemic), pump (cardiogenic), or vessel tone — which is what sepsis and anaphylaxis both destroy, by different routes.

why.q: Shock is defined as a life-threatening, emergency condition
why.t: The definition is about perfusion, not blood pressure. A patient can be in shock while the blood pressure still reads normal, because compensation props it up right until it fails.

why.q: The commonest cause of septic shock is
why.t: The infection is the cause; the shock is the vasodilation it produces. Gram-negative organisms are the classic trigger, through the endotoxin in their cell wall.

why.q: complete C-5 spinal cord transection
why.t: Bradycardia together with hypotension is the tell. Every other kind of shock drives the heart rate up; when a cord injury cuts sympathetic outflow the vessels dilate and the heart cannot speed up to compensate.

why.q: A patient that is in septic shock commonly has
why.t: Early septic shock is warm and fast — vessels dilated, skin warm, heart and breathing racing. Cold clammy skin belongs to hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock, or to sepsis only once it is very late.

why.q: Match each cardiovascular term to its meaning
why.t: Read the endings: -aemia concerns blood, -itis is inflammation, a-systole is literally no contraction. Angina is ischaemia that is still reversible; infarction is when it no longer is.

why.q: Cardiac muscle tissue is distinctive because of their cohesiveness
why.t: Desmosomes hold the cells together; gap junctions let ions pass between them. The stem hands you the first, so the connecting channels must be the second — and that is what lets the myocardium contract as one unit.

why.q: An elderly woman was admitted to the medical unit with dehydration
why.t: Fluid has weight, so acute weight loss is the most reliable measure of how much has been lost. Engorged neck veins and a full bounding pulse are signs of the opposite problem — fluid overload.

why.q: A patient is receiving a loop diuretic
why.t: A loop diuretic strips fluid and electrolytes together, so more than one option here describes a real risk. This key takes the fluid and sodium route (restlessness and agitation); keep the potassium picture — a weak irregular pulse and poor muscle tone — in mind as the same drug's other classic effect.

why.q: Match each respiratory function to its structure or mechanism
why.t: The lungs do a great deal more than gas exchange: speech, smell, pH control and the activation of angiotensin II all happen here. That last one is why the respiratory system keeps turning up in the blood-pressure story.

why.q: For what metabolic reason does respiration occur
why.t: Respiration exists to serve cellular metabolism — oxygen in so the mitochondria can make ATP, carbon dioxide out because it is the waste. Everything else the lungs do is secondary to that trade.

why.q: would not favour internal respiration
why.t: Internal respiration is oxygen leaving the blood for the cells, so it is helped by whatever a hard-working tissue looks like: warm, acidic, high in carbon dioxide. A tissue already rich in oxygen has no gradient left to drive it.

why.q: Match each respiratory structure to its distinguishing feature
why.t: Each one is defined by the job its shape does: the cricoid is a complete ring because it must never collapse, the conchae make air swirl so it is warmed and filtered, and the carina is nerve-rich so anything reaching it triggers a cough.

why.q: Comment on the relative sizes of the two lungs
why.t: The heart sits left of the midline, so the left lung gives up the space — the cardiac notch, and two lobes instead of three. It is also why inhaled objects tend to end up on the right, where the bronchus is wider and steeper.

why.q: The conducting zone includes the nose, pharynx, larynx
why.t: The respiratory bronchioles do not belong to the conducting zone: they already have alveoli budding off their walls, so gas exchange has begun by then. The word that makes this false is all.

why.q: The respiratory zone includes the parts of the lungs
why.t: The rule is simple — if alveoli are attached to it, it is respiratory zone. Everything upstream only moves, warms, filters and humidifies the air.

why.q: only the epiglottis does not have a gaseous exchange function
why.t: Of that list only the alveolus exchanges gas. Trachea, carina and nasopharynx are all conducting structures too, so singling out the epiglottis makes the statement false several times over.

why.q: only the alveolus is in the respiratory zone
why.t: The respiratory bronchiole is in the respiratory zone as well, along with the alveolar ducts and sacs. Again the word only is what makes it false.

why.q: shows the respiratory system parts in the correct order
why.t: Learn it as three stretches: nose to larynx, then the branching bronchial tree narrowing at every division, then the alveolar end where exchange happens. Any sequence question is just testing that map.

why.q: Emphysema is a condition that causes the
why.t: Emphysema destroys the walls between alveoli. Losing that elastic tissue means the lung cannot recoil to push air out, so air is trapped — the problem is expiration, not inspiration.

why.q: At the point where the trachea branches into two bronchiole
why.t: The carina and the cough reflex are both right; the word bronchiole is wrong. The trachea divides into two main bronchi, which are many generations larger.

why.q: The pressure in the alveoli is known as
why.t: Keep the three straight: intrapulmonary is inside the alveoli, intrapleural is in the pleural space and is always the lower of the two, and transpulmonary is the difference between them — the pressure that actually holds the lung open.

why.q: Air is forced out of the lungs during normal expiration
why.t: Quiet expiration is passive: the inspiratory muscles simply stop and the stretched elastic tissue springs back. Muscles are only recruited when expiration is forced.

why.q: During an asthma attack, bronchioles become severely
why.t: Asthma is bronchoconstriction plus mucus and inflammation. Adrenaline relaxes airway smooth muscle through its beta-2 receptors, which is exactly why it is the emergency drug.

why.q: When the trachealis muscle contracts during coughing
why.t: Narrowing the tube makes the same volume of air travel faster, and speed is what shifts mucus. Warming and humidifying happened much earlier, in the nose.

why.q: Infant respiratory distress syndrome occurs because premature infants
why.t: Without surfactant the water lining each alveolus pulls it shut, so the baby has to generate enormous pressure on every single breath. Type II cells only start producing it late in pregnancy, which is what makes prematurity the risk.

why.q: Match each airway level to its wall structure
why.t: Two things change all the way down the tree: cartilage disappears and the epithelium gets thinner, until the alveolar wall is a single flat cell — thin enough for gas to cross in a fraction of a second.

why.q: Match the terms found in the alveoli with their correct function
why.t: Two cell types, two jobs: type I is the thin wall gas crosses, type II makes surfactant. The macrophage is the cleaner, because everything inhaled that got past the cilia ends up here.

why.q: Using the alveolus diagram
why.t: The respiratory membrane is only three thin layers pressed together — alveolar cell, fused basement membranes, capillary cell. Anything that thickens it, whether fluid in pulmonary oedema or scarring in fibrosis, slows gas exchange down.

why.q: Even the most forceful exhalation leaves air in the lungs
why.t: If the alveoli emptied completely they would stick shut and need enormous pressure to reopen. Residual volume is what keeps them open — and it is also why this is the one volume a spirometer cannot measure.

why.q: match each lung volume or capacity to what it means
why.t: Volumes add up to capacities. Vital capacity is the three you can move — tidal plus both reserves — and residual volume is the one you cannot, so it is never part of vital capacity. Check it on the trace: 500 + 3000 + 1100 = 4600 mL vital capacity, and adding the 1200 mL you can never exhale gives the 5800 mL total lung capacity.

why.q: expired forcibly after maximal inspiration
why.t: Read the wording closely: after a maximal inspiration means the entire usable range in one breath, not just the reserve at one end of it.

why.q: The amount of air that can be inspired above the tidal volume
why.t: Reserve means what is left over beyond a normal quiet breath — inspiratory reserve above it, expiratory reserve below it.

why.q: Match the muscles to their action
why.t: Quiet breathing uses the diaphragm and the external intercostals, and nothing else. The neck muscles, the internal intercostals and the abdominals are recruited only once breathing becomes forced.

why.q: Match each partial pressure to where it is found
why.t: The gradient is the whole point: oxygen falls atmosphere → alveolus → blood → cell and carbon dioxide runs the other way. Alveolar air is poorer in oxygen than the atmosphere because it has been humidified and mixed with the air that never left.

why.q: Two gases contribute to 99
why.t: Air is roughly four-fifths nitrogen and one-fifth oxygen. Carbon dioxide is a trace gas by comparison, which is why atmospheric PCO₂ is so tiny next to the alveolar figure.

why.q: not a factor that promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin
why.t: The real modifiers are the ones that change inside a working tissue — heat, acid, carbon dioxide, 2,3-BPG, and a low oxygen pressure. White cells play no part in oxygen carriage at all.

why.q: Match each value to the correct location
why.t: Arterial blood arrives nearly saturated and leaves the tissues still carrying most of its oxygen. That leftover is the venous reserve — what a tissue draws on the moment it starts working harder.

why.q: Hemoglobin has the highest affinity for which of the following gases
why.t: Haemoglobin binds carbon monoxide far more tightly than oxygen and will not release it. That is why carbon monoxide poisoning suffocates a patient whose skin and blood still look healthily red.

why.q: Hemoglobin molecules are fully saturated when bound to
why.t: One haem group per subunit, four subunits per molecule. Each oxygen that binds also makes the next one bind more easily, which is what gives the dissociation curve its S shape.

why.q: In its relaxed state, hemoglobin tends to
why.t: Haemoglobin has two shapes: relaxed binds oxygen, tense releases it. Anything that makes a tissue acidic or hot pushes the molecule towards the tense form, so the oxygen comes off where it is needed.

why.q: Oxygen is uploaded by the heme groups
why.t: They ride on different parts of the same molecule, so haemoglobin can carry both at once — which is exactly what it is doing on the journey back from the tissues.

why.q: The Bohr effect refers to the change in
why.t: The point of the Bohr effect is that it is self-targeting: the conditions that shift the curve are the conditions inside a hard-working tissue, so oxygen is unloaded precisely where demand is highest.

why.q: The majority of carbon dioxide is transported
why.t: Most carbon dioxide is converted inside the red cell into bicarbonate and then carried in the plasma. That same reaction releases hydrogen ions, which is the link between breathing and acid–base balance.

why.q: Match each control centre to its role
why.t: The rhythm is generated in the medulla and only smoothed by the pons; the phrenic nerve is the wire out to the diaphragm. That is why an injury above the mid-cervical cord stops breathing altogether.

why.q: The pulmonary inflation reflex depends upon stimulation
why.t: The inflation reflex is mechanical: stretch receptors in the airways cut inspiration short before the lung is overinflated. Chemoreceptors watch chemistry, not volume.

why.q: When holding our breath for a long time
why.t: Breathing is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide and the acid it produces, not by falling oxygen. It is also why hyperventilating before a breath-hold is dangerous — it delays the urge without adding meaningful oxygen.

why.q: arterial blood gas results
why.t: Read the three values against each other. The pH is alkalotic, the PaCO₂ is low, the bicarbonate is normal — pH and carbon dioxide moving in opposite directions is the signature of a respiratory problem, and a normal bicarbonate rules the metabolic one out. This past paper marks the answer as metabolic alkalosis; the values as printed do not support that, so learn the rule rather than this key: pH and CO₂ opposite means respiratory, pH and bicarbonate together means metabolic.

why.q: The lungs act as an acid
why.t: Only one direction makes sense: more carbon dioxide means more acid, so ventilation must go up to blow it off. The other three statements all move the wrong way, which is what makes them false.

why.q: Match each influence on breathing to its source
why.t: Breathing has three sets of controllers — voluntary from the cortex, emotional from the limbic system, and automatic from the chemoreceptors. The chemical one always wins in the end, which is why a voluntary breath-hold always finishes with a breath being taken for you.

why.q: Match each stimulus to its effect on breathing
why.t: The exercise one is the surprise: rate and depth rise before the blood gases have changed at all, because the motor cortex and the joint receptors signal the medulla directly. The two irritant reflexes divide by level — sneeze above the larynx, cough below it.

why.q: Match each acclimatisation change to what it achieves
why.t: Every change here does one of two things: carry more oxygen, or deliver it closer to the mitochondria. That is why acclimatisation takes weeks — the adjustments are structural, not just a faster rate of breathing.

why.q: Match each clinical description to its correct term
why.t: The same word-parts again, and the pair worth separating carefully is pneumothorax (air where it should not be) and atelectasis (the collapse that the air causes).

why.q: the major function of the lymphatic system
why.t: By volume the lymphatics are a drainage system — they return the fluid the capillaries leak, which would otherwise become oedema. Immunity is what happens to that fluid as it filters through the nodes on the way.

why.q: The typical fluid replacement for the patient
why.t: Match the fluid to the deficit. Isotonic fluid restores volume without shifting water between compartments; hypotonic fluid is what drives water into the cells, and hypertonic pulls it out. Always check which compartment a question is asking you to refill.

why.q: Axillary lymph nodes are often removed in breast cancer cases
why.t: Breast lymph drains mostly to the axilla, so that is where spread shows up first. Sampling the sentinel node is what spares many patients a full clearance — and the arm lymphoedema that can follow one.

why.q: NOT specifically associated with the lymphatic system
why.t: Bone marrow counts because it is where lymphocytes are made. The kidneys handle fluid too, but by filtering blood, not lymph.

why.q: What is the vein labelled A
why.t: This is where the two systems join: the thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein, handing the lymph back to the bloodstream.

why.q: Lymph flows towards the thoracic cavity due to the positive pressure
why.t: Inhalation creates a negative pressure in the thorax, and that is what draws lymph upwards. Skeletal muscle movement is the other pump — lymph has no heart of its own, which is why immobility causes swelling.

why.q: Match each lymphatic term to its meaning
why.t: Two of these are signs to recognise on sight: red streaks tracking from a wound is lymphangitis, and left shoulder-tip pain after abdominal trauma is Kehr's sign of a ruptured spleen.

why.q: Match each immune cell or structure to its role
why.t: Split them by job: B cells make antibody (as plasma cells) and T cells act on cells — CD8 killing infected ones, CD4 directing everybody else. The dendritic cell is the one that starts the whole thing, by carrying antigen to the node.

why.q: rate of carbon dioxide and oxygen exchange is roughly the same
why.t: Diffusion depends on the gradient and on solubility, and here the two almost cancel. Oxygen has much the steeper partial-pressure gradient, but carbon dioxide dissolves far more readily in the watery film and plasma it must cross, so similar amounts move in the same time. Neither gas is actively transported anywhere in the lung — both move by simple diffusion, which rules out two of the distractors outright.

why.q: trachealis muscle contracts
why.t: The trachealis closes the gap at the back of the C-shaped cartilage rings. Narrowing the tube makes the same air travel faster, and a cough clears mucus only because of that velocity. The rings are what hold the airway open; the muscle exists to make it briefly smaller. Warming and moistening are done in the nose, and swallowing is the oesophagus's own muscle.

why.q: majority of carbon dixoide is transported
why.t: About 70% travels as bicarbonate. Carbon dioxide enters the red blood cell, carbonic anhydrase converts it to carbonic acid, and that splits into H⁺ and bicarbonate, which leaves for the plasma. So the reaction happens in the red cell but the carrying happens in the plasma — one distractor puts the finished product in the wrong compartment. Carbonic acid itself is only a momentary intermediate, never a transport form.

why.q: Pulmonary ventilation is also known as
why.t: Learn the four processes as a set: pulmonary ventilation (breathing — moving air in and out), external respiration (exchange at the alveoli), transport of gases in the blood, and internal respiration (exchange at the tissues). Cellular respiration is a fifth and separate thing — the metabolism inside the cell that consumes the oxygen. Only the first is air movement; the rest are exchange or delivery.

why.q: cells that line the airways of the nasal cavity
why.t: The conducting airways are lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, which is exactly what the mucociliary escalator needs: goblet cells to make the mucus, cilia to sweep it. Remove the cilia and there is no escalator — which is what smoking does. Simple squamous belongs to the alveoli, where a short diffusion distance matters more than cleaning.

why.q: function of alveolar type 1 cells
why.t: Split the alveolar cells by shape. Type I are flat and cover most of the surface, so gas crosses them quickly; type II are rounded and secrete surfactant. Propelling mucus is the job of cilia further up the tree, and phagocytosis belongs to the alveolar macrophage — three different cells with three different jobs, all visible in the same micrograph.

why.q: inspired above the normal tidal volume
why.t: Read it as a position on the spirometry trace. Tidal volume is the quiet breath; the inspiratory reserve is what you can still drag in on top of it, and the expiratory reserve is the same idea downwards. Vital capacity is not a reserve at all — it is the whole usable range, IRV plus TV plus ERV — and 'reserve air' is not a term this course uses.

why.q: Match the letters on the diagram showing different lung volumes
why.t: Work from the trace rather than from the names. The volumes are the four single blocks — tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve, residual — and the capacities are sums of two or more, so they are the tall brackets spanning several blocks. Vital capacity is everything except residual volume; total lung capacity is everything including it. Residual volume is the block that never moves, which is what separates that pair.

why.q: maintain a patent or open airway
why.t: Patent simply means open. The larynx is built of cartilage, so it holds its own shape and cannot collapse inwards. The pharynx is a muscular tube that can. The conchae only swirl and warm incoming air, and the hyoid bone is an anchor for muscles rather than part of the airway wall.

why.q: roughly 99% of the air in the atmosphere
why.t: Nitrogen is about 78% and oxygen about 21%, which leaves barely 1% for everything else — argon, water vapour and carbon dioxide together. That is why carbon dioxide in inspired air exerts so tiny a partial pressure, and therefore why the gradient carrying it out of the blood does not need to be steep.

why.q: true during inspiration except
why.t: Inspiration is the active phase: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the rib cage swings up and out, the thorax enlarges, and because the volume rose the pressure inside falls below atmospheric — Boyle's law — so air flows in. Every other statement is a consequence of that one contraction, which is what leaves the relaxed diaphragm as the odd one out. It describes quiet expiration.

why.q: NOT a factor that promotes oxygen dissociation
why.t: Offloading is triggered by signs that a tissue is working hard: more carbon dioxide, more acid, more heat, and a falling PO₂. All of those shift the dissociation curve to the right and loosen haemoglobin's grip — the Bohr effect — which is how exercising muscle extracts more oxygen from the same blood. White cells are immune cells and appear nowhere on that curve.

why.q: Alveoli are prevented from collapsing
why.t: The threat is surface tension: the water film lining an alveolus pulls it inwards, and the smaller the alveolus the harder it pulls. Surfactant from type II cells breaks up that film and lowers the tension. Shape alone does not save it — which is precisely what neonatal respiratory distress syndrome demonstrates, since those alveoli are the right shape and still collapse.

why.q: nerve that excites the diaphragm
why.t: The diaphragm is skeletal muscle, so it does nothing without a motor nerve, and that nerve is the phrenic — from cervical roots C3, C4 and C5. That is why a high cervical spinal injury stops breathing while a lower one does not. The intercostal nerves supply the rib muscles, and the vagus is parasympathetic to the viscera; neither drives the diaphragm.

why.q: saturated haemoglobin molecule
why.t: Each haemoglobin carries four haem groups, each holding one iron atom and binding one oxygen molecule, so saturation is a count out of four rather than a yes or no. Oxygen binds to the iron, not to the amino acids of the globin chains. Each molecule bound makes the next bind more easily, and that cooperativity is what gives the dissociation curve its S shape.

why.q: lung volume is affected by
why.t: Both, and they work against each other. Elasticity is the recoil that empties the lung; surfactant is what stops that recoil from closing the alveoli altogether. Together they set compliance — how much volume you gain for a given effort — so an option offering either one alone is offering half of the mechanism.

why.q: External respiration is affected by all the following except
why.t: External respiration is diffusion across the respiratory membrane, and diffusion is governed by surface area, membrane thickness, the solubility of the gas and the partial-pressure gradient. Airway resistance is a ventilation problem: it limits how much air reaches the alveolus, not how gas crosses once it is there. Sorting factors into 'gets air there' and 'gets gas across' answers most questions on this focus point.

why.q: respiratory membrane is made up of alveolar cells and surfactant
why.t: The respiratory membrane is everything gas must cross: alveolar epithelium, the fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium — three layers totalling only 0.5–1 µm. Surfactant coats the inner surface and lowers surface tension, but it is not one of the diffusion layers. Omitting the capillary wall is what makes the statement false.

why.q: Normal blood pH is
why.t: Narrower than it looks: roughly 6.8 to 7.8 is survivable, and 7.35–7.45 is the slice the body actively defends. Note that it is alkaline, not neutral — so a pH of 7.2 is an acidosis even though 7.2 is still above 7 on the scale. That single point is the trap in almost every acid-base question.

why.q: very high levels of CO 2 would have a pH of
why.t: Carbon dioxide is an acid in disguise: dissolved CO₂ plus water makes carbonic acid, which splits into H⁺ and bicarbonate. More carbon dioxide means more H⁺, which means a lower pH. Because the cause is the lungs failing to clear it, this is specifically a respiratory acidosis — and running the same chain backwards is what makes overbreathing a respiratory alkalosis.

why.q: blood pH of 7.5 due to vomiting
why.t: The answer key on this card is wrong, and a verbatim card is never edited — it reproduces the question and the key exactly as Canvas served them, so read this one and move on. Vomiting loses gastric acid, leaving the blood relatively more alkaline: that is a metabolic alkalosis. The number says the same thing — 7.5 is above 7.45, and question 1 of this very quiz defines normal as 7.35–7.45, so 7.5 cannot be an acidosis of any kind. Hannetjie's own RESP 3 summary slide lists 'Severe vomiting-loss of acid' under Metabolic Alkalosis. Answer it False in your head, and know why.

why.q: Blood with a pH of 7 is
why.t: Anything below 7.35 is acidotic, and 7 is well below it. The trap is reading 7 as 'neutral', which it is for pure water — but blood is held deliberately alkaline, so water-neutral blood would be a life-threatening acidosis. Acidotic describes the blood; acidosis is the process that made it that way.

why.q: diabetic patient metabolising fates and producing ketones
why.t: Two things make this metabolic rather than respiratory: the acid is produced by metabolism — ketone bodies from fat breakdown when glucose cannot enter the cells — and the lungs are not the cause. Compare the carbon-dioxide questions on this quiz: the same low pH, a completely different origin. Expect deep sighing Kussmaul breathing here, which is the lungs blowing off CO₂ to compensate for an acid they did not create.

why.q: Fast and deep breathing gets rid of more carbon dioxide
why.t: Follow the chain: blowing off carbon dioxide removes the source of H⁺, so pH rises. It is respiratory because the lungs caused it and alkalosis because the pH went up — the two halves of the name answer two different questions, and each distractor gets one half right. This is the panic-attack picture, and the reason rebreathing helps.

why.q: About hemoglobin
why.t: The prefix names what is attached: oxy- oxygen, carbamino- carbon dioxide, carboxy- carbon monoxide, deoxy- nothing at all. Carbamino and carboxy are the two most often swapped, and the difference is clinical: carbon monoxide binds far more tightly than oxygen and will not release, which is what makes it lethal. Heme is the iron-holding part itself, and 2,3-BPG is the red cell's own regulator, loosening the grip so oxygen is handed over to tissues. One caution on the figures printed here: Hannetjie's RESP 3 slide puts the carbamino fraction at 20–30%, not the 10–20% on this card.

why.q: parts of the bronchial tree in the correct order
why.t: Follow the air, and watch the order of the two bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles end the conducting zone — no alveoli, no gas exchange — and respiratory bronchioles begin the respiratory zone, because alveoli start budding from their walls. Terminal comes first even though the word sounds final: it is the end of conduction, not the end of the tree.

why.q: Bronchiole are lined with cuboidal epithelium
why.t: The lining thins as the tube narrows: pseudostratified columnar in trachea and bronchi, simple cuboidal in bronchioles, simple squamous at the alveolus. It thins for the same reason the cartilage disappears — less need to condition and clear the air, more need for a short diffusion distance.

why.q: Bronchi are supported by cartilage
why.t: This is the most useful single landmark for telling the two apart down a microscope. Cartilage holds the larger airways permanently open; bronchioles have smooth muscle instead, so their diameter is adjustable — which is exactly why an asthma attack constricts bronchioles rather than bronchi.

why.q: Penumocytes types 1 and 2
why.t: Only type I is squamous — flat, and thin enough for gas to cross. Type II is cuboidal, and its bulk is the point: it needs room for the machinery that manufactures surfactant. The general rule is worth carrying: a cell built for exchange is flat, a cell built for secretion is not.

why.q: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
why.t: Surfactant production ramps up late in gestation, so a premature lung is structurally present but chemically unfinished. Without surfactant, surface tension wins and alveoli collapse at the end of each breath, so every one has to be reinflated from scratch — which is why the work of breathing becomes unsustainable. It is the clinical proof of what surfactant is for.

why.q: Two gases contribute to 99% of the total atmospheric pressure
why.t: Nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%. It matters because of Dalton's law: each gas contributes pressure in proportion to its share, so nitrogen supplies most of the total pressure at sea level while playing no physiological part at all, and oxygen's roughly one-fifth share is what sets the partial pressure driving diffusion into the blood.

why.q: pressure exerted by each gas in a mixture is proportional to its percentage
why.t: Attach each name to its own idea. Dalton is about a mixture: each gas contributes pressure in proportion to its share. Boyle is about one gas and its container: squeeze the volume and the pressure rises, which is what breathing does. Henry is about a gas meeting a liquid: how much dissolves depends on its partial pressure and its solubility. Two distractors deliberately bolt the right name onto the wrong law.

why.q: rate of CO 2 exchange roughly equivalent to that of O 2
why.t: Solubility is the second half of the diffusion story and the half that gets forgotten. Oxygen has the steeper partial-pressure gradient, but carbon dioxide dissolves far more readily in the fluid it has to cross, and the two effects roughly cancel out. Neither gas is actively transported and neither binds the other in transit — simple diffusion, in both directions.

why.q: External respiration is affected by all of the following factors except
why.t: The three that do belong are the terms of the diffusion equation: membrane thickness, gas solubility and the partial-pressure gradient — with surface area as the fourth. Airway resistance sits one step upstream: it limits how much air arrives, which is ventilation, not exchange. Real lung disease blurs the two; this question deliberately does not.

why.q: majority of carbon dioxide is transported
why.t: Roughly 70% as bicarbonate, 20–30% bound to haemoglobin as carbamino compounds, and only 7–10% simply dissolved. Carbonic acid is not one of the three: it exists for an instant inside the red cell before splitting into H⁺ and bicarbonate. That same reaction is why carbon dioxide transport and blood pH are really one topic.

why.q: amount of air that can be expired forcibly after maximal inspiration
why.t: The passage defines it two sentences before it asks: vital capacity is the sum of the inspiratory reserve, tidal and expiratory reserve volumes — everything you can move, which is exactly what 'forcibly expired after a maximal inspiration' describes. Long stems like this usually carry their own answer, and the skill being tested is finding the definition rather than recalling it.

why.q: Hyperbaric chambers are clinical applications
why.t: Two laws, because the chamber does two things at once. Raising the pressure compresses trapped gas — Boyle — which is how it treats decompression sickness and air embolism. It also forces far more oxygen into solution in the plasma — Henry — which is how it treats carbon monoxide poisoning, where haemoglobin itself is unavailable. Frank-Starling is a cardiac law and is present only as a distractor.

why.q: true of inspiration except
why.t: Every other statement follows from the diaphragm contracting: the thorax enlarges, and because the volume rose the intrapulmonary pressure fell below atmospheric — Boyle's law — so air moves in. Air always follows a pressure gradient; it is never pulled or pushed directly. A relaxed diaphragm describes quiet expiration instead.

why.q: Possible causes of hypoxia
why.t: Hypoxia is too little oxygen reaching the tissues, and altitude is the classic cause: the percentage of oxygen is unchanged, but the total pressure is lower, so its partial pressure — the thing that actually drives diffusion — falls with it. Rapid deep breathing does the opposite. And note the swap in the last option: the oesophagus carries food, so obstructing it does not obstruct breathing.

why.q: inspired above the tidal volume
why.t: Reserve means 'on top of what you already did'. Above a quiet breath in sits the inspiratory reserve; below a quiet breath out sits the expiratory reserve. Vital capacity is the total span of both plus the tidal volume in between, and 'reserve air' is not a term this course uses.

why.q: not a role of the pleura
why.t: The pleura is a two-layered sac wrapping each lung; it is not a partition. The thorax is divided into left, right and mediastinum by anatomy the pleura sits inside rather than by the pleura itself. The other three options are genuine: serous fluid removes friction during breathing, each sealed sac limits infection spreading from one side to the other, and the negative intrapleural pressure it maintains assists venous return to the heart.

why.q: NOT a factor that promotes oxygen dissociation
why.t: The factors that loosen haemoglobin's grip are all markers of a hard-working tissue: rising carbon dioxide, rising acidity, rising temperature and falling PO₂. Three of the four options are on that list. White cell count is an immune measure and never appears on the dissociation curve — which identifies it as the odd one out even if the rest will not come to mind.

why.q: trachealis muscle contracts it reduces the diameter
why.t: Narrowing the trachea forces the same air through a smaller opening, so it travels faster — and a cough shifts mucus only because of that velocity. The cartilage rings are C-shaped, open at the back, precisely so the trachealis can draw the ends together. Warming and moistening happen in the nose, and moving food is the oesophagus's own muscle.

why.q: majority of Oxygen is transported in the blood
why.t: About 98.5% rides on haemoglobin and only around 1.5% dissolves in the plasma — which is why anaemia causes tissue hypoxia even when the lungs are working perfectly. Two distractors are traps of wording: oxygen binds as a whole molecule rather than as ions, and carboxyhaemoglobin is haemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide, not to oxygen.

why.q: Quiet expiration is a passive process
why.t: Quiet expiration is the one phase of quiet breathing that costs nothing: the inspiratory muscles simply stop contracting, and the stretched lung and chest wall spring back. Stretching them during inspiration is what stored the energy in the first place. Expiration only becomes active when it is forced — then the abdominal and internal intercostal muscles take over.

why.q: Quiet inspiration is an active process
why.t: Both muscle groups, and the diaphragm does roughly two-thirds of the work: it flattens downwards while the external intercostals lift the ribs up and out. Quiet inspiration is always active, and that asymmetry against a passive quiet expiration is the whole point of the pairing.

why.q: Forced exhalation is an active process
why.t: Notice the intercostals appear in both directions under different labels: external intercostals lift the ribs to breathe in, internal intercostals pull them down to force air out. The abdominal muscles add to it by driving the viscera up against the diaphragm. Any statement pairing 'external intercostals' with expiration has them the wrong way round.

why.q: Forced inhalation involves the contraction of the following muscles
why.t: These are the accessory muscles of inspiration, and they are worth knowing as a clinical sign rather than as a list: a patient recruiting neck and shoulder muscles to breathe is visibly in trouble. Each one works by lifting some part of the rib cage or sternum, enlarging the thorax beyond what the diaphragm alone can manage.

why.q: Ventral Respiratory Centre is involved in the forced expiration
why.t: The first sentence is correct and the second is not, which makes the statement as a whole false. The dorsal group drives quiet inspiration — it sets the basic rhythm and fires the diaphragm and external intercostals. The ventral group is largely silent during quiet breathing and switches on when demand rises, driving forced inspiration and forced expiration. So forced inspiration belongs to the ventral group, not the dorsal one.

why.q: tracheal carina is the most sensitive area
why.t: The carina is the ridge where the trachea divides into the two main bronchi, and it is the most cough-sensitive point in the whole airway. That makes sense as a last line of defence: anything reaching it is about to enter a lung. It is why suctioning to that depth provokes violent coughing, and why an inhaled object lodging there is an emergency.

model.q: Where in the body are B- and T- lymphocytes made and stored
model.t: The memory hook is B for bone marrow, T for thymus — both cell lines are made in marrow, and only the T cells travel to mature. Write made, mature and stored as separate statements: the marking points are awarded separately for each.

model.q: What is the structure of a lymph nodes
model.t: Three marks, three parts: capsule, contents, function. Adding that a node has more vessels coming in than going out — so flow slows and the macrophages get time to filter it — shows why the structure suits the job.

model.q: Which cells in the body will find antigens in the body
model.t: The phrase worth writing down is antigen presenting cells. Dendritic cells belong in that group too, though the marking points name macrophages and B lymphocytes.

model.q: Which cells will stimulate a full on immune response
model.t: Keep the sequence in the answer: present, then T cells organise, then B cells make antibody. The marks are for the mechanism, not for naming the cells.

Two halves, and the second is the one that gets forgotten under pressure: answer vaccination in general (the antigen without the disease, memory cells stored) and then the mRNA mechanism specifically. Herd immunity is worth a line.

model.q: What is the difference between vaccination and immunisation
model.t: One mark each way: vaccination is the act, immunisation is the result. Noting that immunisation can also follow the infection itself makes the distinction unmistakable — and it is why a vaccine can fail.
